title_original: When Newcastle Dreamed of Being the Brasilia of the North
excerpt_original: Newcastle Contemporary Art brings together two photographic archives, one from the industrial Northeast, the other from East London, to tell fifty years of working-class neighborhoods remade and rehousing promises broken. L’article When Newcastle Dreamed of Being the Brasilia of…

blocks.caption: Scotswood Road, October 1963 © T Dan Smith Archive / AmberSide Collection (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: Newcastle Contemporary Art brings together two photographic archives, one from the industrial Northeast, the other from East London, to tell fifty years of working-class neighborhoods remade and rehousing promises broken.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos: Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust.

blocks.caption: Killingworth, Modern Housing, 1980. © Lambdon Visual Aids (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: Twelve hundred Victorian houses in the working-class district of Byker, in Newcastle, were condemned as unfit for human habitation in 1953, then torn down from 1966 onward, brick by brick. Among the residents were photographers, who documented the erasure of their own streets. “ Under Development: What Happens When Cities Change?” gathers their prints and traces Britain’s great building schemes from the sidewalk rather than the drafting table.

blocks.caption: Eldon Square and Carpark, 1980. © Lambdon Visual Aids (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)
Eldon Square Interior Shopping Precinct, 1980. © Lambdon Visual Aids (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: Two activist collectives kept this journal. Amber, founded in London in 1968 and settled in Newcastle the following year, trained its lens on brick back lanes, backyards and the flowered pinafores of the industrial North. The other workshop, opened in 1973 in Bethnal Green, in the working-class East End of London, pursued the same inquiry among the laboring families and immigrant communities settling there.

blocks.caption: Eldon Square Interior Shopping Precinct, 1980. © Lambdon Visual Aids (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)
Maryam, Byker Revisited, 2007 © Sirkka-Liisa Konttinen (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: Alongside prints by Henri Cartier-Bresson, his wife Martine Franck and Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide, the exhibition brings together the work of Jimmy Forsyth, a Welsh laborer blinded in one eye by a splinter of chisel in 1943 and left without a job. The Byker works, meanwhile, dragged on for thirteen years. Rehoused elsewhere in the meantime, four families out of five built new lives far from the neighborhood.

blocks.caption: Eldon Square, 1980. © Lambdon Visual Aids (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)
Tselmuun, Byker Revisited, 2004. © Sirkka-Liisa Konttinen (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: A political section closes the show, devoted to T. Dan Smith, Newcastle’s Labour council leader in the 1960s, who promised to turn the city into “the Brasilia of the North.” Smith photographed the streets he was tearing down: in one of his slides, a man turns to look back across the rubble, before a gutted schoolhouse. A twist of fate? Caught in a corruption scandal and convicted in 1974, he went to prison before ending his days in one of the Cruddas Park towers, built under his own administration.

blocks.caption: Stephanie, trainee nurse, with fiancé Stephen, Byker Revisited, 2005. © Sirkka-Liisa Konttinen (Courtesy of the AmberSide Trust)

blocks.text: The show “Under Development: What Happens When Cities Change?” runs through November 28, 2026 at Newcastle Contemporary Art , admission free.
